blogs.title: When Threats Aren’t Persecution: The Tenth Circuit’s High Threshold in Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: This post unpacks the panel’s rigorous approach to the persecution element, emphasizing how repeated death threats, armed confrontations, a menacing schoolyard incident involving a child, and significant psychological distress still did not cross the line into “persecution.” We situate the ruling within Tenth Circuit precedent (Karki, Ritonga, Wiransane) and compare approaches in other circuits to explore whether the Tenth is entrenching a particularly demanding threshold—especially when physical injury is absent. The piece offers takeaways for evidentiary development when cases rest on cumulative threats and emotional harm.

blogs.title: Politics or Payback? Mixed-Motive Nexus and the ‘One Central Reason’ Test
blogs.description: Focusing on the nexus analysis, this post examines how the court parsed political animus from criminal retaliation. Despite Petitioners’ Liberal Party activity, the court credited evidence that the threats escalated only after Jimenez jeopardized a narco-trafficker’s operation—framing the harm as retribution for exposing criminality (“snitch”) rather than political opinion. We analyze the panel’s use of the mixed-motive framework (Rivera-Barrientos; O.C.V. v. Bondi) and identify what kinds of record evidence can elevate political opinion from “tangential” to “central”—including persecutor statements, timing, and links between political work and the harms.

blogs.title: Unwilling or Unable, or Just Unreported? The Reporting Requirement After Singh v. Bondi
blogs.description: This piece examines the court’s unwilling-or-unable analysis and its heavy emphasis on reporting to authorities. Leveraging Singh v. Bondi, the panel faults Petitioners for minimal engagement with law enforcement and treats isolated police apathy as insufficient to show systemic failure. We explore the evidentiary contours of the futility/danger exception, how to build a record proving government complicity or incapacity (including beyond one-off conversations), and the risks of relying on general country conditions without tying them to concrete efforts—or documented barriers—to seeking protection.

blogs.title: Relocate and Deny: Internal Relocation as a Backstop in Colombian Narco Cases
blogs.description: Even assuming future risk, the court held that Petitioners could safely relocate within Colombia, citing unharmed relatives, a prior safe stay in the countryside, and threats limited to their neighborhood. This post analyzes the burden framework for relocation, the role of national reach evidence for criminal groups, and how reasonableness is assessed when economic and administrative obstacles are raised but thinly briefed. We consider the practical implications for Colombian claims involving narco-traffickers allegedly tied to political actors, and what practitioners must show to defeat the relocation prong.
